# Choice screens are not market choice

A choice-screen proposal starts with an appealing promise: require a dominant platform to show people several services instead of steering everyone to its own. But the central question is not whether a list appears. It is who designs the list, sets its order, writes its labels, and controls what happens after the click. A screen can display alternatives while leaving the gatekeeper’s power intact.

Start with selection. If the platform operator decides which products qualify (the listed options), it can turn admission into a private regulatory system. Rules that sound neutral—minimum scale, technical compatibility, security review—may favor established firms with compliance teams and existing integrations. Smaller developers don't merely compete for users; they first compete for permission to be seen. The catalog looks open, but its shelves still belong to one company.

Placement matters too. A default (the option already selected) isn't a decorative detail. It saves a step, avoids uncertainty, and tells the user what the system considers normal. Preinstallation, highlighted buttons (the brightest route), and repeated confirmation prompts can do the same work. An alternative buried behind extra taps doesn't meet the default on equal terms—it begins the race several meters behind.

What happens when you choose a rival? If the gatekeeper can warn, delay, re-prompt, or limit access after the selection (the post-choice path), the apparent decision won't travel very far. Developers may gain a logo on a screen yet remain dependent on interfaces, permissions, and commercial terms controlled by the same firm. Nominal choice does not become market choice merely because the first page contains more icons.

This is why disclosure alone can't cure structural control. The company that owns the doorway can still decide who approaches it, how wide it opens, and which route is marked “recommended” (the privileged label). That power affects product design before any user sees the screen. Developers may build toward the gatekeeper's criteria, avoid features that invite review, or abandon distribution altogether—choices made under pressure rather than in a free market.

A meaningful remedy would separate presentation from control. Eligibility rules should be public, narrow, and tied to functions the screen actually serves (basic compatibility and security). The operator should not be free to exclude a rival because its business model threatens the operator's revenue. Decisions need reasons, prompt appeals, and review by an independent authority—not another team inside the same gatekeeper.

The remedy must also govern defaults. Initial placement could be randomized or rotated (without paid preference), labels should follow a common format, and every option should take comparable effort to select. Once a person chooses, the platform should honor that decision across relevant entry points. It should not keep asking until fatigue produces the answer the platform wanted in the first place.

Portability and interoperability matter because selection without exit is thin protection. Users need practical ways to move settings, data, and relationships (the things that create switching costs), while developers need stable access to documented interfaces on fair terms. This doesn't require freezing a platform's design or forbidding legitimate safeguards. It requires safeguards that cannot double as a quiet veto over competitors.

Enforcement also has to reach retaliation. A platform shouldn't be able to comply on the screen and recover its advantage elsewhere through slower approvals, degraded features, or discriminatory fees (the off-screen penalty). Clear anti-circumvention rules matter here. Otherwise the remedy becomes a painted door—visible to everyone, usable by nobody—and developers bear the cost of proving each new obstruction from scratch.

Measurement should follow outcomes rather than screenshots. Regulators should examine whether selections persist, whether rivals receive equivalent technical treatment, and whether smaller developers gain meaningful routes to users (mere impressions). A remedy may look tidy at launch and still fail under the daily pressure of product updates and policy changes. If it won't alter incentives, it won't alter the market.

We should judge choice screens by whether they transfer power, rather than whether they add another menu. We need rules that constrain selection, neutralize defaults, protect a chosen alternative, and make exit realistic—backed by audits (independent tests), appeals, and enforceable consequences. Lawmakers and platform operators should demand no less: the remedy must change who controls the path, because a gatekeeper-curated choice is still gatekeeping.
